questions.question: What are variadic functions in Go?
questions.title: Variadic Functions
questions.direct_answer: func sum(nums ...int) — the function receives nums as a SLICE ([]int). Call with any count: sum(1,2,3), sum(), sum(slice...) (spread a slice). The ... is the variadic marker, on the parameter and on the spread.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: func sum(nums ...int) — the function receives nums as a SLICE ([]int). Call with any count: sum(1,2,3), sum(), sum(slice...) (spread a slice). The ... is the variadic marker, on the parameter and on the spread.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The variadic parameter collects arguments into a slice:

```go
func sum(nums ...int) int {
    total := 0
    for _, n := range nums { total += n }
    return total
}

sum(1, 2, 3)   // 6 — three separate args, collected into []int{1,2,3}
sum()           // 0 — zero args, empty slice
sum([]int{4, 5}...)  // 9 — spread an existing slice
```

Executed. Inside the function, nums IS a []int — the same loop, indexing, len, slicing as any slice.

The rules: exactly ONE variadic parameter, and it must be the LAST. func f(a string, nums ...int) is legal (fixed args first); func f(nums ...int, a string) is a compile error.

The spread operator (...) — the same symbol, different position: in the declaration it means 'collect'; at the call site after a slice it means 'expand.' The pair composes: variadic collection + spread = passing slices through.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[sum 1 2 3] --> C[collects into slice]
    S[slice...] --> E[expand into args]
    C --> F[nums is []int]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What it's for: printf-shaped APIs (fmt.Println takes ...interface{} — any count of anything), option patterns, builders. What it's NOT: the only way to pass slices — the spread form means a slice-based call is always available.

The interface{} variadic: func log(args ...interface{}) — any count of any type. fmt's whole API is built on this — and so is every print-shaped helper you've written.

questions.question: How does the spread operator work with variadic functions?
questions.title: When would you use Variadic Functions in a real project
questions.direct_answer: slice... at the call site expands the slice's elements as individual arguments. sum(slice...) == sum(slice[0], slice[1], ...). The elements are passed — the callee still receives them as a (new) slice.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: slice... at the call site expands the slice's elements as individual arguments. sum(slice...) == sum(slice[0], slice[1], ...). The elements are passed — the callee still receives them as a (new) slice.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Executed both sides:

```go
func sum(nums ...int) int { /* sum the slice */ }

nums := []int{1, 2, 3}
sum(nums...)   // == sum(1, 2, 3) — the slice expands into args
sum(4, 5)      // direct call — no slice needed
```

The spread and the direct call produce identical callee state — a []int containing the elements. The spread is the bridge when your data is already a slice: logWithPrefix(msg, parts...), append(dst, src...).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[sum 1 2 3] --> C[collects into slice]
    S[slice...] --> E[expand into args]
    C --> F[nums is []int]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two uses of the SAME symbol, which is the confusion to clear: in a signature, ...T means 'collect these arguments into a slice.' At a call site, s... means 'expand this slice into arguments.' Declaration collects; call site expands. Every built-in that takes lists works this way — append(slice, items...) is the canonical example: append's second parameter is variadic, and the idiom appends a whole slice via spread.

The immutability/copy subtlety worth one sentence in an interview: the variadic slice you receive is a NEW slice (the runtime allocates and copies the arguments — except in the spread-of-existing-slice optimization, where the runtime MAY pass the original — which is why modifying a variadic parameter is a style bug: the caller may or may not see the changes).
